# glTF models

@difference Extension: `LoadMesh` and `LoadAnimMesh` also read glTF 2.0 files, and `LoadTexture` and `LoadImage` read the pictures inside them.

`LoadMesh` and `LoadAnimMesh` read glTF 2.0 files with the cgltf library (an extension: the original has no glTF): `.gltf` files, which are JSON with the data in files next to them or inside as `data:` uris, and `.glb` files, which hold the JSON and the data in one file. The file type is told by what is in the file, not by its name. `LoadMesh` makes one mesh of the model as it looks without animation, `LoadAnimMesh` keeps every node as an entity with the animation of the file and works with [Animate](Animate), [SetAnimTime](SetAnimTime), [FindChild](FindChild) and [LoadAnimSeq](LoadAnimSeq).

* glTF is right-handed with y up, Blitz3D is left-handed with y up, and both have the front of a model at +z. The conversion mirrors x: positions, normals and translations change the sign of x, rotations are mirrored with them, and two corners of every triangle change places (the front of a Blitz3D face is where its corners go around the other way). A model that faces +z in glTF faces +z here, and its left hand stays on its left. The vertices of a surface come in the order that the faces use them. The pictures of glTF start at the top, as those of Blitz3D do, so the texture coordinates are not changed. The unit is what the file says (glTF says meters).
* Every node is an entity with the name of the node, its translation, rotation and scale (or its matrix, without a skew), below one entity at the top that stands for the scene. A node that has a mesh is a mesh entity. The `scene` of the file is loaded, or the first one, or everything if the file has none. Lights (`KHR_lights_punctual`: directional, point and spot) and cameras of the file are entities too: each is a child of the entity of its node, named like the light or camera (or `<node> light` / `<node> camera`) and turned half a turn, so that it looks along the file's -Z in the same way as in other glTF viewers. A light keeps its color, range and the cone angles of a spot light (the intensity is not used). A camera is made with `CameraProjMode 0`, so that it does not draw over the camera of the program until you switch it on with `CameraProjMode`; its zoom comes from the field of view and its range from `znear` and `zfar`.
* A mesh with more than one primitive has a surface for each material. Triangles, triangle strips and fans are read; points and lines are not. Indices of 8, 16 and 32 bits, and positions, normals, two sets of coordinates (`TEXCOORD_0` and `TEXCOORD_1`), vertex colors (`COLOR_0`, with or without alpha, set on the vertices, `EntityFX` 2 shows them) and the quantized integer forms of these (`KHR_mesh_quantization`) are read. A primitive without normals gets smooth ones made. Tangents and morph targets are not used.
* A material becomes a brush: `baseColorFactor` is the color and alpha, `baseColorTexture` the picture, `1 - roughnessFactor` the shininess, `doubleSided` is `EntityFX` 16 and `KHR_materials_unlit` is `EntityFX` 1. The alpha mode `OPAQUE` ignores the alpha of the color, `BLEND` gives the picture an alpha channel (flag 2) and `MASK` cuts it out (flag 4, at an alpha of one half whatever `alphaCutoff` says). `KHR_texture_transform` (offset, rotation and scale, and `texCoord`) is put into the texture coordinates of the vertices, and the sampler's `CLAMP_TO_EDGE` wrapping becomes the clamp flags 16 and 32 (mirrored wrapping is a repeat). The picture is found next to the model, as for every model; `.png` and `.jpg` are what glTF uses, the formats of [Image formats](Image-Formats) work as well, and `EXT_texture_webp`, `EXT_texture_avif` and `KHR_texture_basisu` are tried when a texture has no `source`.
* Blitz3D has one picture for a brush: the metallic-roughness, normal, occlusion and emissive textures are not used, and neither are the emissive color and `KHR_materials_emissive_strength`. Roughness and metalness are only the shininess. A normal map would need the tangent space, which the lighting of Blitz3D (Dot3) does not have, so it is left out on purpose.
* A node with a `skin` is skinned: each vertex has up to eight joints (`JOINTS_0` and `JOINTS_1`) with their weights (`WEIGHTS_0` and `WEIGHTS_1`), which are made to add up to 1, and the joints are entities that [Animate](Animate) moves. The node's own place is left out for a skinned mesh, as glTF says. The inverse bind matrices of the file say how the vertices go into the space of each joint; a joint that several skins use has the matrix of the first one that names it.
* The animations move the translation, rotation and scale of nodes (not weights). Time is in seconds, one second is 60 frames. The first animation starts at frame 0; with more than one in a file, each starts one frame after the one before it and `AnimLength` is the end of the last. They are one animation with several sequences: sequence 0 is everything and sequence 1, 2 and so on are the animations of the file in their order. A node that an animation does not touch is at its starting pose while the animation plays. `LINEAR` is interpolated (rotations on the shortest way), `STEP` holds until the next key, and `CUBICSPLINE` is evaluated at eight places between keys.
* The pictures inside a glTF file can be loaded with `LoadTexture` and `LoadImage`: `LoadTexture("model.glb")` gives the first picture of the file, `LoadTexture("model.glb#2")` the third (the numbers are those of `images` in the file). The picture can be a `data:` uri, a view of a buffer or a file next to the model, and 0 is the result if there is no such picture. `LoadAnimImage` and the other commands that load a picture file read them the same way.
